steps.title: Как это работает
steps.html:
Для общей способности в прошлом обычно could: She could read at four.

Для конкретного случая, когда получилось, используют was able to или managed to, а не could.

В отрицании правило мягче: couldn't подходит в обоих случаях — I couldn't open the door.

Be able to нужна там, где у can формы нет: I'd like to be able to…, I've never been able to…, You'll be able to…

steps.title: The children who waited
steps.html:
A test with a marshmallow seemed to predict how children’s lives would turn out. Fifty years later, researchers are still arguing about what it really measured.

A  The experiment could not have been simpler. A researcher put a marshmallow on a plate in front of a four-year-old and made a promise. “If you can be patient and wait until I come back, you can have two.” Then he left the room. What happened next was filmed, and the films are still difficult to watch: children who could not resist covered their eyes, turned their backs, sang to themselves, and sat on their hands. Most of them gave in before the fifteen minutes were up.

B  The psychologist behind it, Walter Mischel, began this work at Stanford University around 1970. He was not really interested in marshmallows. He wanted to measure something much harder to see: whether a small child could hold on to a reward that was not there yet. The successful children were not the ones who stared at the plate and made an enormous effort. They were the ones who managed to turn their attention away from it — and if you succeed in doing that, Mischel argued, you may forget about the temptation altogether.

C  Years later, his team went back to the same children, who were now teenagers. The results were striking. Those who had been able to wait longer had better exam results, coped better with stress, and were described by their parents as more socially confident. The study became one of the most famous experiments in psychology, and its conclusion spread far beyond the laboratory: teach children to wait, and you improve their lives.

D  Then, in 2018, a team led by Tyler Watts repeated the study with a much larger and more varied group of children. They found something more complicated. Children who waited did tend to do better later — but once the researchers took the family’s income and education into account, most of the difference disappeared. A child from a secure home has good reasons to trust a promise. A child who has learned that promised things often do not arrive has good reasons to eat the marshmallow now.

E  This does not mean the original experiment was worthless. It was probably measuring two things at once: the ability to resist, and the experience that makes resisting seem sensible. In one version of the test, researchers deliberately broke a promise to one group of children before the marshmallow appeared. Those children waited, on average, about a third as long as the others. They had not become less patient. They had simply stopped believing the researcher.

F  So what should we take from it? Not that some children are born to succeed and others are not. Mischel himself always insisted that waiting is a technique rather than a personality: you can teach a child to look away, to think about something else, to make a plan. What the newer research adds is a second, less comfortable point. Before you can ask a child to wait for a reward, somebody has to make sure the reward actually comes.

Written for this course. Based on published accounts of Walter Mischel’s Stanford experiments (from 1970) and on Watts, Duncan and Quan, Psychological Science, 2018.
